Land acknowledgement

We are on unceded
Algonquin Anishinaabe territory.

Ottawa sits on land the Algonquin people have never given up by treaty, sale or surrender.

Unceded no treaty, ever 36,000 km² under claim, including Parliament Hill Since 1992 still negotiating

space or → to advance · F fullscreen · N notes · ? help

Unceded: no treaty was ever signed for the Ottawa valley, so under the constitution Aboriginal title was never surrendered or acquired by the Crown. The Algonquins of Ontario claim (negotiating since 1992, Agreement-in-Principle 2016, no final treaty yet) covers about 36,000 km²: Parliament Hill, Algonquin Park and all of the City of Ottawa. Nearest Algonquin communities: Pikwàkanagàn at Golden Lake (about 150 km west) and Kitigan Zibi at Maniwaki (about 130 km north); nine more along the Ottawa River in Quebec. Source: Crown-Indigenous Relations, Algonquins of Ontario land claim page.
Who was where · about 1600
Before
  • Omushkego CreeHudson and James Bay lowlands
  • AnishinaabeOjibwe and Saulteaux: Superior, the north shore of Huron, the northwest
  • AlgonquinOmàmiwininì: the whole Ottawa River watershed
  • OdawaManitoulin and the Bruce Peninsula
  • WendatHuron: farming towns between Georgian Bay and Lake Simcoe, 20,000+ people
  • TionontatiPetun: the Blue Mountains
  • AttawandaronNeutral: Niagara to the Thames

Boundaries are approximate. Nations moved, traded and overlapped, and this is one snapshot just before European disease and war reshaped the south. Cree, Anishinaabe and Algonquin are also the three largest Indigenous languages still spoken in Ontario.

Ask: where would our school be on this map? (Inside the Algonquin area, near the bottom right.) Point out that the south was dense farming country (Wendat towns of a thousand or more people) while the north was hunting and fishing territory, which is why the dots on the next slide look the way they do. Territory shapes are drawn from standard historical atlases (e.g. Historical Atlas of Canada, native-land.ca) and are deliberately soft-edged.
Where they are now · 2026
Now

139
First Nations in Ontario today, on 207 reserves covering under 1% of the province
28
communities you can only reach by air, or by winter road for a few weeks a year
  • Wendat, Tionontati, Attawandaron dispersed by 1650; Wendat now at Wendake, Quebec
  • Haudenosaunee arrived 1784: Six Nations, Tyendinaga
  • Mississauga, Chippewa moved south c. 1700, then surrendered it, 1764–1923
  • Cree, Oji-Cree, Ojibwe still in the north, on reserves, under Treaties 3, 5, 9
Wendat descendants also live in Oklahoma and Kansas (Wyandotte). Six Nations and Tyendinaga are now the two largest First Nations in Ontario. The southern surrenders are the Upper Canada treaties (1764–1862) and the Williams Treaties (1923). The dots are band office locations from Indigenous Services Canada. Amber dots are the fly-in communities (no all-season road): almost all of them in Nishnawbe Aski Nation territory under Treaty 9, between Sioux Lookout and the James Bay coast. Compare the south: many nations, tiny reserves. Compare the north: the same nations as 1600, on their lands, but with an airstrip as the only way in or out.
1 of 7 · clean water

Boiling water since 1995

Neskantaga: the longest boil-water advisory in Canada. Ontario still has 27 long-term advisories in 26 First Nations.

Neskantaga First Nation
Neskantaga (pop. about 300) has been under a boil-water advisory since February 1995; its water plant has never worked properly. Ontario has 27 long-term advisories in 26 First Nations (ISC, Sept 2026), 14 of them in fly-in communities. Kashechewan's plant failed in January 2026 and most of its 2,200 people were flown out for weeks. Bill C-37, the First Nations clean water act, was introduced June 2026.
2 of 7 · a dyke that can fail

Kashechewan lives behind a dyke

Built on the Albany River floodplain, the community has been evacuated for flooding most springs since 2006. A 2019 agreement to move it to higher ground is still unbuilt.

Kashechewan First Nation from the air
Kashechewan sits on the Albany River floodplain behind an aging ring dyke; engineers called it at "horrible risk of collapsing" in 2015. The community has been evacuated for spring flooding repeatedly (2006, 2008, 2012–2019, 2022, 2024), often by Canadian Forces Hercules. A 2019 agreement promised relocation to higher ground at Site 5; it has not happened.
3 of 7 · housing

Housing

Attawapiskat has declared a state of emergency five times since 2006. In 2011, families were living in tents, sheds and trailers.

Attawapiskat First Nation
Attawapiskat declared a housing emergency in 2011 with families in uninsulated tents, sheds and trailers, many homes full of black mould. It has declared states of emergency five times since 2006. Census 2021 / CMHC: 30% of on-reserve households in Ontario are crowded and 44% of homes need major repairs.
4 of 7 · housing

Homes inside the dyke

Three in ten homes on Ontario reserves are crowded and 44% need major repairs. Floodwater like this means mould, and the federal housing advocate calls it a "spiralling cycle".

Kashechewan First Nation, spring flooding
Federal Housing Advocate, Aug 2026: 165 emergency events hit 134 First Nations in 2025 and more than 40,000 people were evacuated; displacement lands on pre-existing housing and infrastructure gaps. Census 2021 / CMHC: 30% of on-reserve households in Ontario crowded, 44% of homes needing major repairs.
5 of 7 · evacuations

Leaving again

January 2026: Kashechewan's water plant failed and most of its 2,200 people were flown out for weeks. June 2025: 2,000 flown out of Sandy Lake as a wildfire closed in.

Boarding an evacuation flight
The Red Lake 12 fire (about 170,000 ha) forced Sandy Lake and Deer Lake out; the Hercules could not fly full because the airstrip is too short. Across Canada the 2025 season displaced more than 40,000 First Nations people from 83 communities (Federal Housing Advocate, Aug 2026). Namaygoosisagagun (Collins), Ontario, lost its homes.
6 of 7 · the winter road

A road for six weeks a year

Trucks on the frozen Albany River. The rest of the year, everything comes by plane.

Moosonee–Attawapiskat winter road, 2004 · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
28 Ontario communities have no all-season road. Fuel, building materials and bulk food arrive on winter roads that open for a few weeks and are shortening as winters warm; otherwise by air. A 10 kg bag of flour costs $40–70 in Neskantaga; a healthy diet costs about 86% more than in Thunder Bay (SLFNHA food-costing report).
7 of 7 · health and school

"We need a nursing station"

Neskantaga youth meet the Ontario Ombudsman, 2025. For high school, they leave home at 14.

Neskantaga First Nation, 2025 · Ricochet Media / Jon Thompson
Grade 10 is the last grade offered at home in the 23 remote communities served by the Northern Nishnawbe Education Council; students board in Thunder Bay or Sioux Lookout. Seven students died in Thunder Bay between 2000 and 2011 (Tanya Talaga, Seven Fallen Feathers). Nishnawbe Aski Nation has recorded more than 560 suicide deaths since 1986; four in ten were youth. Crisis line 1-844-NAN-HOPE. Anything serious medically means a medevac flight.

All nine are Liberal MPs elected 28 April 2025. Mail to any MP is postage-free: House of Commons, Ottawa ON K1A 0A6. Find your riding by postal code at ourcommons.ca/members. Neighbourhood lists are rough guides; contact details from ourcommons.ca, October 2026.

A letter to an MP is a concrete action a class can take. Suggest one concrete ask: support the First Nations clean water bill (Bill C-37, introduced June 2026), or ask what the member is doing about long-term advisories. The Prime Minister's constituency office is by appointment only; the PMO publishes no phone number, so use the web form or the parl.gc.ca email.
